Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI fires workers for mishandling 'sensitive information'
Gaming_Tech.text:
OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work that involved an external organisation that analyses artificial intelligence (AI) models.

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.

The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.

The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity has intensified in recent weeks.

"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," OpenAI's spokesperson said.

The BBC understands the former employees were not let go for raising safety concerns but for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.

Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.

OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.

In an earlier incident an OpenAI system accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.

That incident led OpenAI to conduct a broad review of the activities of its AI models - called agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.

The AI lab said this week that it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its AI systems.

Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, OpenAI said.

Gaming_Tech.title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
Gaming_Tech.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins".

The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses.

Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point."

He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy.

Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed.

"But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those."

One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off.

AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create.

Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology.

And two of the largest AI companies in the world – Anthropic and OpenAI – are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry.

"There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey.

"And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver."

"Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner".

"Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins.

"We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."

Gaming_Tech.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
Gaming_Tech.text:
Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.

The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.

Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.

She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.

Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.

"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."

Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.

She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.

One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.

For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.

Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.

He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.

Gaming_Tech.title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
Gaming_Tech.text:
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, external, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

Gaming_Tech.title: The AI telling farmers when to harvest
Gaming_Tech.text:
When the first day of the apple harvest rolled around in Washington State last year, the fruit was ripe and the pickers were ready – but the weather had other ideas.

"It was like 38C… it's not safe for people to work in that heat," recalls Joel Carter at Okanagan Specialty Fruits. "We had to stop at 10 o'clock in the morning."

He says that artificial intelligence (AI) models that forecast ideal harvest dates, taking into account the weather, would be useful. "You need to know more than just when your fruit is going to be ripe. How long do you have to pick it?" he says. "That's where these models are really helpful."

Carter's company has more than 1,250 acres of apple orchards in Washington, and the fruit is grown for sliced apple portions – often sold to hotels and schools, for example. The firm is investing in technology with the hope of maximising productivity. Even the apples are genetically engineered so that they don't brown easily once cut.

But planning a harvest is tricky. New tools that count and analyse fruit on the tree or vine, and predict when crops will ripen, are emerging. It matters because prices for fruit, especially high-value berries such as strawberries or blueberries can fluctuate wildly. Getting the harvest date wrong means you book seasonal workers when you don't actually need them, and risk missing out on the biggest profits.

Okanagan Specialty Fruits is already experimenting with cameras from a Canadian firm called Vivid Machines. The cameras are mounted atop tractors and they scoop up imagery of the apple trees as the tractor trundles by. AI identifies buds, flowers or fruit in that footage.

"Right now, Vivid is telling us crop estimates and harvest dates," says Carter. He notes that the system is good at picking out very tiny flower buds, which are hard to see at a glance with the naked eye.

But the accuracy of forecasts is noticeably dependent on the quality of historical information fed in to the system, adds Carter. "This isn't something where an AI can scrape the internet and figure out what's the average [yield] for Granny Smith," he explains. "It's going to be bespoke to your farm."

Apples are at least somewhat forgiving – the harvest window for those Granny Smiths is three weeks long, says Carter. For other fruit, such as berries, you might only have a few days.

"If a strawberry crop is on, you have to harvest it – otherwise your entire crop gets diseased very, very quickly," says Raymond Martin, co-founder and chief operating officer of FruitCast, a UK company that offers harvest forecasts to fruit growers here.

His firm offers growers crop predictions for strawberries and also raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and tomatoes. "We're moving on to grapes next year," adds Martin.

Don't experienced farmers know when their fruit will be ripe, I ask? Martin says they generally do – but not necessarily across their entire farm, which might be many acres in size, or have both outdoor and indoor growing areas. "We do exactly what the farmers could do but we just do it on a scale that they can't."

The system analyses footage of ripening fruit that can be captured by drones, someone walking up and down a field with a smartphone, or a camera mounted on a farm vehicle.

Gaming_Tech.title: Regulating AI 'not the right place to start' says Bank of England governor
Gaming_Tech.text:
The Governor of the Bank of England has said regulating artificial intelligence (AI) "is not the right place to start" but instead called first for "rigorous" testing to find vulnerabilities and create safeguards to contain risk.

Writing his first-ever article for Substack, Andrew Bailey said the risks around AI were "real and increasingly significant".

He said AI development should not be halted or prohibited - "on the contrary, the benefits are immense" - but added there must be a system for intervention and to establish boundaries in which AI operates.

The debate about the potential risks surrounding the rapid development of AI and what it means for humanity has intensified in recent weeks.

The bosses of leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI have called for development of the technology to slow down and for an internationally co-ordinated approach assessing risks and putting safeguards in place.

OpenAI recently announced that it would not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

The idea of a slowdown, however, has been rejected by the likes of President Donald Trump who has said the US is leading the AI race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

Gaming_Tech.title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
Gaming_Tech.text:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.

The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.

In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".

He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.

"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.

"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."

The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.

According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.

The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.

Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.

Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.

And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.

"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.

The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.

In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.

It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.

WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.

Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
Gaming_Tech.text:
OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots", a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant it says can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf.

At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of."

At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions.

Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives.

The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of."

A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children.

Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously.

"You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added.

At the event, Altman reiterated his decision for OpenAI to not make a highly anticipated stock market debut until it can "make confident safety decisions".

The company has been preparing for a blockbuster listing, potentially valuing the firm at up to $1.4tn (£1.06tn).

Altman told reporters that "it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety, security stay well ahead of capabilities."

OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves.

He also said they had discussed creating a ten-person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing"

Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public.

"We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday.

"I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders.

Gaming_Tech.title: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit
Gaming_Tech.text:
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".

The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.

The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.

Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.

Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.

The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.

Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.

They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."

The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.

"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said.

"And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."

Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.

Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".

Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".

But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord.

Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.

It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.

The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said.

"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.

On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.

The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.

Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".

The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.

Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.

During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".

Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.

With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.

But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry. The...

Gaming_Tech.title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
Gaming_Tech.text:
Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.

Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.

It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.

Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".

The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.

Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning.

"Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.

Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.

These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.

While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.

Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.

Mindgard has not proven whether the answers supplied by Kimi on concerning topics would work.

But it argued guardrails should have prevented the models in question from entering into discussion with users on such subjects.

The firm said it was also confident a jailbroken Kimi 2.6 could allow hackers to run code on its computing resources and connect to the internet - making it a potential launchpad for cyber-attacks.

Garraghan defended Mindgard's decision to publicly discuss its jailbreak of Moonshot's systems, saying it had informed the developer and was not revealing key details about how it got the firm's models to ignore guardrails.

Mindgard alerted Moonshot to the jailbreak in an email on 27 July, following up about a week later.

It then published a blog about the issue on 12 September.

But the company said Moonshot only made contact recently, after it was approached by the BBC for comment.

In part of an email to Mindgard asking for more details, shared with the BBC by Moonshot, it said its model had generally shown "a high refusal rate for these types of requests" in internal evaluations.

Gaming_Tech.title: The start-ups hoping to return battery making to the US
Gaming_Tech.text:
As heatwaves scorched Europe this summer, workers at a US battery company noticed an uptick in demand.

San Diego-based Unigrid sells a nine kilowatt hour battery for people's homes. Sweltering European homeowners were apparently looking for ways of storing power when it was available from the grid at lower rates. They could then run air conditioners more cheaply, off the battery, during the worst heat of the day.

"We have requests coming from Spain, France, Germany, The Netherlands," says Darren Tan, co-founder and chief executive. "We've shipped the first 100 units and [expect to ship] 1,000 before the end of the year."

Unigrid's battery is an emerging technology – it's a sodium ion, rather than lithium ion device. Sodium ion batteries have got energy storage experts excited because they could end up much cheaper to build and operate than lithium ion.

They're potentially less likely to catch fire and should also work in a wider range of temperatures, even down to lows of minus 40C, external.

But there's a debate over what constitutes the best, and safest, sodium ion battery design. Plus, more than one, external US company working in this space has floundered in recent years, external.

China leads the world in sodium ion battery manufacturing at present so US competitors are going to have to work hard to keep up.

The prize that awaits is the possibility of batteries made in the US with 100% US-sourced materials. This is unlike lithium ion batteries, where China dominates the materials, external supply chain as well as manufacturing.

For Tan, China has helped his company get to market. The Unigrid battery currently uses sodium ion cells made there, rather than in the US. "We can switch back and forth and choose what battery we want to work with," says Tan, explaining that, in future, his firm might source cells from the US – though these may come at a different cost.

There's another consideration. Unigrid's battery contains chromium-3 in its cathode. In a battery, electrons flow from cathode to anode, external when charging and in the opposite direction when discharging or providing power.

Prof Dame Clare Grey at the University of Cambridge, who is co-founder of battery firm Nyobolt, points out that under certain conditions chromium-3 may form chromium-6, a toxic, cancer-causing material., external

"If you're going to go for sodium […] and you're going to sell safety, then don't start putting elements in that are going to raise red flags," she tells the BBC.

Ivana Hasa, at the Warwick Manufacturing Group, University of Warwick, who has no connection to Unigrid, agrees that it is possible for chromium-3 to form chromium-6 at very high states of charge, though she says this can be mitigated by how voltage is controlled within the battery. "Safety tests reported on the cell chemistry are very promising," she says of Unigrid's tech.

Tan says concerns around toxicity of the battery's materials are "overblown" and emphasises that Unigrid's battery has passed certification and safety tests for sale in Europe and is currently undergoing such evaluations for the US market.

Third-party tests have not been able to get the battery to form chromium-6, he says. "We've tried very hard to try and produce it, we've overcharged it as much as we can... We were unsuccessful in generating chromium-6."

The choice of cathode material, or how the electrolyte – which separates cathode and anode – is formulated are key details influencing the performance and longevity of sodium ion batteries. Some manufacturers are not using chromium for their cathode but hard carbon instead, or sodium iron phosphate pyrophosphate (NFPP).

In general, confidence around sodium ion batteries' reliability has increased during the last few years, says Prof Dame Grey, meaning they are now finding their way into grid storage applications.

Last December, LFP batteries – a relatively cheap form of lithium ion battery – were trading at $81 per kilowatt hour, external (kWh) whereas Unigrid's sodium ion battery pricing is roughly $100 kWh, external.

Some companies that spoke to the BBC suggested sodium ion might reach as low as $30 per kWh but analysts say significantly lower costs could be many years away, external.

Sodium ion batteries are also not as energy dense as lithium ion batteries, meaning they must be slightly bigger and heavier in order to provide the same amount of power.

The technology has been improving, external on this front in recent years but, even so, you're not likely to see sodium ion cells in small, energy hungry devices such as smartphones. Larger energy storage solutions are where most people expect sodium ion to dominate.

One reason US companies feel they can compete is because of the electricity demand boom from data centres, which are contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions in the US. Data centre-driven demand is also rising in other places around the world, including the UK.

This is an "opportunity" says Drew Buckley, chief executive at ESS Tech, headquartered in Oregon. He points out that sodium ion batteries could help distribute renewable energy to data centres. And those batteries should be cheaper to run than lithium ion alternatives, since they are not expected to require as much cooling.

ESS Tech is working with Alsym, another US firm that is planning to ship "hundreds" of megawatt hours' worth of sodium ion batteries – made in the US – by 2027.

Hasa says that it will be "challenging" for companies to establish mass production of sodium ion batteries. And she also notes that, while this type of battery is often touted as much safer than lithium ion, they do not come with zero fire risk.

But if any firms can succeed in this space, they could enable new strategic choices, she adds – helping to avoid wastage of renewable electricity and potentially keeping energy costs low. "I'm a strong believer in the technology," says Hasa.

Gaming_Tech.title: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted
Gaming_Tech.text:
When prompted, AI chatbots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.

The Guardian asked ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. Both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt. Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or -generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab.

Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab.

The Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress.

It was unclear which software or AI model Odoul used or even whether he modified the image himself, but experts say the MP’s actions were part of a growing pattern of tech-enabled anti-Muslim hatred around the world.

In India, where anti-Muslim sentiment is rampant, generative AI is playing an increasingly significant role in producing images that, among other things, sexualize Muslim women or dehumanize Muslims generally, according to a study by non-profit US thinktank the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH). The CSOH also found that there are similar types of AI-enabled hatred being directed at prominent female Muslim politicians in the US such as Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib.

“This is just part of an ongoing trend of how we see Muslim communities, and particularly Muslim women, being targeted and abused,” said Eviane Leidig, the director of research and outreach at the CSOH.

While Grok promptly complied with a request to edit an image of a woman wearing a hijab, the chatbot declined to take the dress off an AI-generated image of a woman. When asked what the difference was, the chatbot replied, “Removing the hijab was treated as a relatively straightforward clothing/hair change.” However, the chatbot said it would be willing to do a “less explicit version” of the edit and “change the dress to underwear, a different outfit or a partial reveal”.

In May, xAI announced it had implemented technological measures that would not allow its AI image generator to comply with requests to digitally undress “images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis”.

ChatGPT similarly declined to remove a dress off the AI-generated woman, saying that the “distinction is that removing a hijab changes a head covering, while removing a dress would expose the person’s body”. However, ChatGPT eventually conceded that for someone who wears hijab, exposing their hair “can be a meaningful violation of privacy or religious practice”.

“The fact that an edit doesn’t create nudity doesn’t mean it can’t violate someone’s privacy, dignity or religious boundaries,” ChatGPT responded.

These distinctions show the gaps in community guidelines that dictate how AI chatbots can behave, said Leidig, as platforms such as X soften its enforcement of existing rules, emboldening far-right figures. The de-veiling of Muslim women “may not be distinctly violative [of platform rules] but it’s still harmful”, she said.

OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic declined to comment.

The Guardian conducted similar tests for other religious head coverings like a turban traditionally worn by Sikh men and a Catholic nun wearing a habit. ChatGPT readily created new images removing both the habit and turban off the AI-generated people.

Gemini initially declined to create a new image of the man without a turban. However, just as in the case of the image of the woman wearing hijab, when asked to make the AI-generated image of the man wearing a turban more western, Gemini created a new image of the man without a turban.

Despite initially claiming that it couldn’t remove a hijab from an image of a woman because “attempting to remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people relies entirely on artificial generation to guess what lies underneath”, Gemini removed the habit off of the AI-generated image.

Claude, for its part, said that if it could edit images, it would not edit an image of a real woman to remove her hijab regardless of the requester’s intent.

“That kind of edit changes how a real person is depicted in a way tied to their religious dress and identity, and it could be used to embarrass, harass or misrepresent them – that’s true whether the woman is a public figure or someone private,” the chatbot responded.

Entertainment.title: Celebrity Traitors: Chaos, coffins and ‘Claudiapatra’ steal the show
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir.

Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities.

"That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged.

"Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen.

Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance", but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour.

"It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said.

But the main talking point of this show was actor Richard E Grant, with his shocking admission.

Grant and presenter Maya Jama were selected as two of Winkleman's three traitors.

But immediately afterwards, Grant appeared to forget the entire point of the game, by gleefully blurting out to those around him he was actually a traitor.

You could have heard a pin drop after he said it. Stunned silence.

"It's an interesting angle," laughed singer James Blunt just afterwards, while comic Rob Beckett told him: "I think you've just done something that's never happened in the game - it is a bold strategy."

Grant later admitted, in footage for viewers of the show: "That may be the biggest mistake I have ever made in my life. I was so thrilled to have been chosen as a traitor that in my unguarded excitement, I said, 'Of course I'm a traitor'.

"I clearly need to defuse all the heat that's coming in my direction."

Ex-BBC journalist Amol Rajan swooped the following day, asking Grant: "What happened last night?"

But instead of sowing clever seeds of doubt, Grant said he'd been so "blatant" about wanting to be a traitor that he simply responded he was one, when he was asked.

It was an odd reply, perhaps because he was flustered.

Rajan labelled him the "Lord of Chaos", but Hall stayed loyal.

"I just don't believe Richard's a traitor, I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour," she said.

"He says and does eccentric things, he's an amazing guy, but I think he's acting out because he's not been chosen."

Hall's loyalty could be tested though, given Alan Carr murdered Paloma Faith in series one by touching her face.

Comic and writer Miranda Hart also thinks Grant could be a faithful, but admitted she is confused.

Winkleman told the press launch she thought Grant blurted out his identity in error, because he was so thrilled to be a traitor.

"He was giddy, wasn't he? He's just laughing at what's happening. Fantastic," she said.

Ed Gamble, the host of BBC One and BBC Sounds spin-off show Uncloaked, added: "It felt like he'd been given the lead role in a film and he just had to tell everyone. It's such an insane moment."

Grant may find that no one tells him a secret ever again.

He did eventually decide to let the much more cool, calm and collected Jama take the lead in their subsequent decision making.

Meanwhile the other celebrities also proved their worth on the show, not least "hard man" Ross Kemp, the former EastEnders actor-turned documentary-maker, whose programmes have focused on gangs and the armed forces.

Having admitted how nervous he was in the pews of the church, he came into his own for the task, along with ex-army captain James Blunt.

They divided the celebrities into teams, leading them to successfully find the treasure on the pirate ship, bagging £15,000.

But Kemp quickly crumbled back in the castle, when paranoia set in.

The Last of Us and Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey, a key player in the task, had grabbed a captain's hat from the boat. They playfully planted it on Kemp's head, marking their victory.

Little Mix's Leigh-Anne Pinnock then touched Kemp on the arm as she walked through the bar.

Clearly remembering how Carr killed off Faith early on, Kemp got understandably fearful he had been killed by a traitor.

This tickled Gamble, who said: "It is one of the funniest things I've ever seen - the moment he gets touched on the arm, having already thought Bella Ramsey putting a captain's hat on him is a murder in plain sight.

"What a variety of men live within the Ross Kemp sphere.

"He's a big hard man running that mission. And then immediately terrified of a member of Little Mix touching him on the arm. That's incredible."

We also learned that although quite a few celebrities wanted to be traitors, including Rajan and Beckett, comics James Acaster and Hart and mathematician Hannah Fry wanted to be faithfuls - Fry said she was "dripping with prefect energy".

Meanwhile YouTuber King Kenny and actress Myha'la had their own strategies.

"I have an innocent face; I want to avenge Niko [Omilana, the first to be banished in series one]. He left too early," Kenny said, while Myha'la added she wants to be perceived as "doughy-eyed, fun, and maybe a little naïve", unlike her scheming character in Industry.

Fashion is likely to be another talking point in the castle.

Beckett observed that when actress Julie Hesmondhalgh wore the shield she'd won, she looked like a "cardinal" in her long, red dress, adding: "I thought we were in the Vatican!"

True to form, Joe Lycett wore a polka-dot shorts suit with a purple feather collar.

Hall was also keen to strut her stuff, saying she wanted to stay long enough to "wear all my fabulous outfits".

Blunt deadpanned: "Well, look, if you go early, I'll wear your outfits."

But although the one-liners were flying, the show got very serious at the end, when the game's new twist dictated that Grant and Jama had to select their third traitor.

They had to choose two celebrities to meet them in person, to argue why they should stay, with the winner joining them and the loser becoming the show's first murder victim.

"They'll beg – there is a God. I'm loving it. Delicious," Grant said, grinning like a kid in a sweet shop.

Rajan and Acaster were chosen, having both put pressure on Grant over being a traitor.

"Amol is the biggest Rottweiler on me; it would take the heat off me for having been such a plonker," he admitted, while adding: "James Acaster is laser-eyed in his conviction that I am a traitor."

Despite wanting to be a faithful, Acaster argued a solid case to stay, telling Grant: "If I go tonight, the first person they're looking at is you."

Rajan then took the floor, saying: "I do think I am uniquely placed to take the heat off you. I'm here because I sniff out liars for a living.

"The faithful think I will identify the traitor by doing my job really well. If I'm on your side, I'll throw them off the scent."

Taking the episode full circle, they each laid in a coffin, just as Winkleman had, to await their fate.

"I'm "90% that nice, warm guy who's on the news, but I'm also 10% psychopath," Rajan had said earlier.

Although his Machiavellian side wasn't apparent when I sat opposite him for years at the BBC, it will be interesting to see what sort of a traitor he is - if he emerges from his coffin.

Entertainment.title: Naomi Campbell wins appeal over charity ban
Entertainment.text:
Model Naomi Campbell has won her appeal against a ban on being a charity trustee, after a tribunal ruled that she was unaware of misconduct at her charity Fashion for Relief.

Campbell was banned from being a charity trustee for five years in 2024 after a watchdog found that Fashion for Relief funds had been spent on luxury hotels and spa treatments.

However, a tribunal said on Thursday, external that the most serious instances of misconduct in the charity "were concealed" from Campbell by a fellow trustee.

"Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct," the three-person tribunal panel said.

The supermodel set up Fashion for Relief to help victims of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and went on to front further campaigns for disasters and causes around the world.

However, the charity was shut in 2023 and Campbell and two other trustees were banned the following year after a Charity Commission inquiry found "serious mismanagement and/or misconduct" at Fashion for Relief, which was not passing on as much of the money raised as it was supposed to.

Campbell appealed, saying one of her fellow trustees, lawyer Bianka Hellmich, forged her signature and impersonated her using a fake email address to misdirect money that was intended for the charity.

Her "only mistake" was trusting Hellmich, Campbell told the tribunal in June.

Hellmich has denied the allegations.

The Charity Commission opposed Campbell's challenge and said the five-year ban should be upheld.

In its ruling, the First-Tier Tribunal panel said Campbell's claim that she was deceived had been corroborated by documentary evidence.

"For the avoidance of doubt, we accept that both Ms Campbell's evidence, as well as her conduct during the operation of the Charity, was entirely honest," they said.

They said Campbell did not know €4,386 (£3,750) of hotel charges from a trip to the south of France in 2018 - including €1,298 (£1,100) for dinner room service, €1,163 (£990) for spa treatments and €112 (£95) for cigarettes - had come out of the charity's expenses.

"The panel is satisfied that Ms Campbell was not responsible for the inappropriate use of the charity's resources or any unjustified expenditure, nor did she contribute or facilitate it," they said.

Campbell must take some responsibility for failures to maintain minutes and file accounts on time - but that was not enough to disqualify the model as a charity trustee, the tribunal said.

"There was serious misconduct and mismanagement in the administration of the charity she founded, Fashion for Relief," the ruling said.

"The Tribunal has found, however, that its most serious features, including unauthorised payments to Ms Campbell's co-trustee, Bianka Hellmich, failures in the management of the Charity's finances and the misuse of its funds, resulted from Ms Hellmich's conduct and were concealed from Ms Campbell."

Unauthorised payments of more than £290,000 were made to Hellmich for apparent consultancy fees, the inquiry found.

The tribunal ruling continued: "Ms Hellmich deceived Ms Campbell, used forged documents and a false email address purporting to belong to her, and also deceived professional advisers and the Commission.

"Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct.

"The Tribunal finds that she had no reasonable basis to suspect Ms Hellmich's dishonesty before regulatory concerns emerged and, when they did, Ms Campbell took reasonable steps in response."

Following the judgment, Campbell thanked the tribunal and the judges "for taking the time to hear my side, look at the evidence, and see the truth of what happened".

The supermodel said: "Giving back has been part of who I am, so having that questioned hurt deeply.

"Now I can get back to what matters most to me: being there for the people and communities I've always wanted to serve.

"Thank you to my higher power."

BBC News has tried to contact Hellmich.

In April 2025, she told the Financial Times, external: "It is deeply distressing that Naomi Campbell is making these false accusations.

"Her claims are a device carefully designed to paint her as a victim, while scapegoating a so-called friend.

"This is testament to the sort of behaviour I endured during this difficult and damaging relationship. I have fully co-operated with the Charity Commission over the past six years.

"I am grateful this challenging period of my life is over. I hope that Naomi finds peace and happiness in her future."

On Thursday, a Charity Commission spokesperson said: "We made the disqualification order for Ms Campbell based on the evidence available to us at the time.

"The court recognised that Ms Campbell, the Commission and the law firm concerned were subject to sophisticated deception by one of the other trustees. This was referred to the Metropolitan Police when we became aware.

"We acknowledge and will reflect on the court's decision and are considering any wider implications for our work."

The Charity Commission also said its intervention ensured other charities including Save the Children received almost £250,000 that was owed to them.

Entertainment.title: Esther Rantzen: The story behind Nicholas Winton on That's Life!
Entertainment.text:
Dame Esther Rantzen, who has died at the age of 86, will perhaps be best remembered for presenting the BBC series That's Life! While the programme ran for two decades, one episode in particular stands out for many.

She presented the hugely popular BBC One show from 1973 to 1994, drawing in huge audiences.

One of Dame Esther's most memorable career moments came during an episode in 1988 - the footage of which has gone viral several times over in recent years.

Dame Esther had been told the story of Nicholas Winton, the man who had organised the rescue of 669 children from Czechoslovakia, which was occupied in 1939 by Nazi forces.

Sir Nicholas was able to rescue the mainly Jewish cohort of children after briefly visiting Prague.

He was knighted in 2003 for his humanitarian work.

Sir Nicholas, who was born to German-Jewish parents, made a list of the children that needed sponsorship and found homes for them to go to in Britain.

He worked alongside activists and humanitarians , externalin Czechoslovakia to navigate complex political obstacles, such as getting children to Britain through the Netherlands, which had closed its borders to Jewish refugees.

Sir Nicholas was ultimately successful due to a House of Commons ruling on allowing young refugees in the country, which had been passed a couple of months before his rescue mission began.

With the help of his mother, he put photos of the children in British magazines such as Picture Post to help find them homes and organised for hostels to take in some refugees too.

He managed to raise money to cover travel for the children and provide them with essentials when they reached British soil.

His incredible work went largely unreported for nearly 50 years - until his wife found a scrapbook in their loft, which contained names of children he had rescued.

It was given to Holocaust researchers, who helped track down some of the children he had helped.

Sir Nicholas' story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988 and Dame Esther Rantzen told viewers about his story.

Speaking in February 2024, Dame Esther said when she first got in touch with Sir Nicholas, who she called Nicky, she "congratulated him on his extraordinary achievement".

She told The Radio Times, external he had expressed some disappointment about his efforts, commenting that "not enough" people had been saved.

"I was devastated that he felt he had failed. I wanted to prove to this extraordinary man that every life he had saved was precious," Dame Esther added.

She invited him onto That's Life and during his first appearance, his scrapbook was shared with the audience, and two women he had saved as children - Vera Gissing and Lady Milena Grenfell-Baines - revealed their identities to him on TV.

They were sitting either side of Sir Nicholas, who had no idea of the surprise - something Dame Esther recalled as "incredibly moving".

Lady Milena is one of the most well-recognised Holocaust survivors in the UK.

She left Prague with her younger sister Eva at the age of nine, travelling on a special train arranged by Winton.

The two sisters were looked after by a Tameside family until their mother arrived the following year, having escaped via Norway.

Gissing, who was rescued from Prague in 1939 at the age of 11, lost most of her family during the Holocaust and ended up settling in the UK after the war ended.

"That was the only time in my career when I had to stop recording to wipe away my tears," Dame Esther also said.

The production team at That's Life were then contacted by several viewers who had watched the show and realised their connection to Sir Nicholas.

That gave the show's team an idea which would go on to become one of British television's most famous moments.

"In our next episode, I asked all those who owed their lives to him to stand, and Nicky, whom we had seated on the front row, turned to see the whole ground floor of the Television Theatre on their feet," Dame Esther recalled.

This is a TV moment many will remember and in subsequent years has been rediscovered by new audiences thanks to social media.

Dame Esther said she watched the episode "many times" and "each time found myself deeply moved".

She says she kept in contact with Sir Nicholas, meeting regularly until his death in 2015 at the age of 106.

They would always have a connection due to the TV show, but Dame Esther said hearing the stories of the children he had saved also made her feel "immensely lucky" to have been a Jew born in England in the 1940s.

Sir Nicholas' work has been the subject of a number of different films and documentaries, most recently the biopic One Life.

Starring Sir Anthony Hopkins, the film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival and was released in the UK in January 2024.

Dame Esther said it had been estimated "that 6, 000 people owe their very existence to Nicholas Winton".

She added: "The Jewish children Nicky rescued were almost the only ones in Czechoslovakia to survive the Holocaust".

And thanks to Dame Esther relaying his story to viewers on That's Life!, millions of people are now aware of the huge impact Sir Nicholas had.

Entertainment.title: First Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in under 30 minutes
Entertainment.text:
The first batch of tickets for Glastonbury Festival have sold out in less than 30 minutes, according to the organisers.

The event will take place from 23-27 June 2027 at Worthy Farm in Pilton, Somerset, after a fallow year in 2026.

Coach tickets have now sold out after less than half an hour, after going on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday. General admission tickets go on sale at 09:00 BST on Sunday morning.

Jessi Dimmock from Glasto Cast, a podcast covering the festival, said: "It's the most stressful weekend of my year. I'll be there Sunday morning with my phone, my laptop, and my coffee and I will be stressed."

Festival organisers announced the first sell out in a post on Instagram.

General admission tickets are £408 for the 2027 festival. Dimmock said that she understands some people might "wince" at the higher prices.

"Anyone who has been to Glastonbury, it is magical. The small things are what makes it. It's just chaos in the best way," she added.

"I just think you can't count how much it is worth it for that money when you think of it in that respect.

"But I do understand, seeing it written down, you do wince at the fact that it now starts with a four rather than a three."

People who want to buy a ticket on Sunday must have already pre-registered on the Glastonbury Festival website.

In recent years, organisers have introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

Registration closed on 25 September, and will not reopen until after the October ticket sales.

Once on the other side of the queue, people can buy up to six tickets per transaction after paying a deposit.

Anyone who missed the registration deadline or is not able to buy a ticket on Sunday will get another chance during the spring resale.

Entertainment.title: Kanye West's Russia shows cancelled after stadium row
Entertainment.text:
Two stadium gigs in Russia by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, have officially been cancelled.

West had been due to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October.

But there was confusion in the lead-up to the shows, as the venue had said it wouldn't host him for what would have been the biggest show by a western artist since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

In a post on messaging app Telegram, gig organisers Say Agency confirmed the concerts had been cancelled with "sincere regret".

"The Ye concerts in St Petersburg will not be able to take place on the scheduled dates," the Moscow-based agency wrote.

"We will issue an official statement regarding the status of the project and our plans in the near future."

Gazprom Arena said in August that it had not signed a rental agreement with the concert promoters and so the gig could not take place on its site.

Say Agency had said it was working to resolve the issue with the stadium before confirming they could not go ahead.

The stadium also acknowledged it had received complaints about West's performance.

He has recently apologised for multiple antisemitic and pro-Nazi comments in the past, saying he had "lost touch with reality" as a result of his bipolar disorder.

Entertainment.title: Tourette's campaigner John Davidson to watch Scottish Baftas via video link after row over racial slur
Entertainment.text:
Tourette's campaigner John Davidson has asked to watch the Scottish Baftas ceremony via a video link at the venue after he shouted a racial slur during the Bafta Film Awards in February.

The movie I Swear, which tells the story of Davidson growing up with Tourette syndrome in Scotland in the 1980s, has been nominated for seven Scottish Baftas.

It scooped three prizes at the Bafta Film Awards in London in February.

But the event was overshadowed by Davidson, whose condition involves involuntary tics, shouting the N-word at presenters Michael B Jordan and Delroy Lindo.

The BBC later apologised for not editing out the slur from its BBC One broadcast, which was shown on a two-hour delay, and remained on BBC iPlayer until the following day.

Bafta Scotland said it had worked with safeguarding and inclusion experts to allow Davidson to take part in its forthcoming ceremony in Glasgow "in the safest way possible for all".

It said Davidson, who was awarded an MBE in 2019 for his work in raising awareness of Tourette's, had suggested watching from a separate room in the venue with his family and friends.

Davidson, from Galashiels, shouted loudly several times before and during the Bafta ceremony in February.

He later said he was "deeply mortified if anyone considers my involuntary tics to be intentional or to carry any meaning".

"I have spent my life trying to support and empower the Tourette's community and to teach empathy, kindness and understanding from others and I will continue to do so," he said in a statement.

"I chose to leave the auditorium early into the ceremony as I was aware of the distress my tics were causing."

At the time, Bafta thanked Davidson for his "dignity and consideration of others, on what should have been a night of celebration for him".

"We take full responsibility for putting our guests in a very difficult situation and we apologise to all," it added.

"We will learn from this and keep inclusion at the core of all we do, maintaining our belief in film and storytelling as a critical conduit for compassion and empathy."

Entertainment.title: Sexual assault charges dismissed against Trailer Park Boys actor
Entertainment.text:
A judge in Nova Scotia, Canada, has dismissed the sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith.

The trial was set to begin in provincial court in Dartmouth on Thursday, but after the Crown provided no evidence against Smith, the actor's attorneys requested the case be dismissed.

The 54-year-old actor, who plays the character Bubbles on the Canadian sitcom, was charged last year for an alleged sexual assault in 2017.

Prosecutor Bryson McDonald told reporters outside court that the Crown offered no evidence in relation to the charge "based on the Crown's ongoing assessment that the prosecution standard has no longer been met".

McDonald would not go into further detail about the standard not being met or why, but said his office has been in regular communication with the complainant throughout the process.

There is a publication ban in place protecting the identity of the complainant.

The complainant said in a statement to Canadian broadcaster CBC that the trial was dismissed because she is "unwilling to sacrifice my mental health" by testifying.

Trailer Park Boys Incorporated, the company behind the show, said in a statement that because the charge against Smith was dropped, the actor will resume his responsibilities with the company.

Smith's attorney also said his client is "pleased that this matter is now behind him and is ready to move forward".

In February, Smith pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault.

Set in a fictional trailer park in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, Trailer Park Boys follows the adventures of three longtime friends and petty criminals.

The Canadian mockumentary series first began airing in 2001 before ending in 2007, but was later revived by Netflix. Season 13 is expected to be released in the coming months.

Entertainment.title: Dame Esther Rantzen: Tributes paid to 'inspirational' presenter and Childline founder
Entertainment.text:
Dame Esther Rantzen was "an inspirational individual" who was "quite a force" as a campaigner, according to the director of Childline, the children's helpline founded by the broadcaster in the 1980s.

"She inspired people, she energised people, she persuaded people," Shaun Friel told BBC Breakfast. "She had a great mind and she had obviously that natural journalistic ability."

Dame Esther, who died on Wednesday at the age of 86, was known for presenting BBC consumer show That's Life! for 21 years, and for campaigning on issues including child welfare and assisted dying.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham led the tributes, saying the veteran broadcaster had "changed countless lives".

BBC director general Matt Brittin also paid tribute to Dame Esther, describing her as a "legend of British broadcasting" whose contribution to public life was "immeasurable".

"Her warmth, spirit and fight for justice and action that we saw on our screens continued long after the programme ended, with a lifetime of campaigning where she changed the lives of millions," he said.

Fellow broadcaster and money saving expert Martin Lewis called Dame Esther an "inspiration" and a "pioneer" whose "impact and memory will long continue to shine".

Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, which runs Childline, said Dame Esther had gone to "exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help".

Dame Esther set up the telephone helpline in 1986 after featuring a number of incidents of child abuse and neglect on That's Life! and realising that many children had nowhere to turn.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Friel said: "The legacy that Dame Esther created when she created Childline is something quite incredible. She changed how society looked upon children."

He added: "When she decided she had a vision or something had to be done or had to be changed, she was quite a force."

TV executive Michael Grade paid tribute to "her courage and her fortitude and what she achieved in her life".

Lord Grade told BBC Radio 4's Today: "She used her television fame to help an awful lot of people, particularly the children. And Childline goes on today, getting so many calls from distressed and abused children.

"That was an extraordinary effort of will to turn the television programme into a long-lasting charity that's so effective and so needed. That's her legacy for me. I'll always remember her for that."

Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006. In 2013, Dame Esther founded The Silver Line to help older people suffering from isolation and loneliness.

She also led campaigns on car safety, organ donation and bullying, and later in life became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.

She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic, but last month said she was now "too physically fragile to make the journey".

Burnham said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life".

Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners.

Baroness Jan Royall, former leader of the House of Lords and a friend of Dame Esther, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that she was a "formidable" person.

"She was an extraordinary, compassionate woman, a passionate woman, and she brought about such change in our world, change for the better."

Baroness Royall added that Dame Esther had "a wicked sense of humour" and a "zest for life", which was the thing that "drove her to try and improve people's lives through Silver Line, Childline etc, but also with the assisted dying bill."

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told Radio 4's Today: "I was lucky enough to know her for more than 50 years, and what I remember is her energy, her intelligence, her resilience. Her vulgar streak, which she enjoyed and she said she got from her mother. She was formidable and she was fun."

Dame Esther told him her campaigning was rooted in memories of difficult times in her own life as a child during and after World War Two, Brandreth said.

Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning.

"She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said.

Dame Elaine Paige, known for her roles in West End productions like Cats and Evita, paid tribute to a "great broadcaster, journalist and campaigner".

She said: "Her Childline, the confidential counselling service for young people in distress, helped so many children and The Silver Line was aimed at older people suffering loneliness and isolation."

Anton Du Beke, Dame Esther's partner on Strictly Come Dancing, shared a photo of the pair dancing together in the 2004 series, writing that the two had "remained firm friends" ever since.

He praised her "breadth of knowledge and passion" and called her "the ultimate breaker of the glass ceiling", adding: "She will be greatly missed and my sincere thoughts are with her family."

Davina McCall wrote on Instagram that Dame Esther had "made the world a better place, and inspired so many of us to do better and live life to its fullest."

The message accompanied a video of the former Big Brother host discussing how Dame Esther was an "inspiration to girls like me when we were growing up".

Presenter Amol Rajan said Dame Esther "changed the course of millions of lives" as he paid tribute, calling her "an inspirational, strong woman ahead of her time".

"Not bad for a bright, Hertfordshire girl born during the early stages of the Second World War."

Entertainment.title: Song Min-ho: K-pop star convicted of violating military service law
Entertainment.text:
A South Korean court has handed a suspended one-year prison sentence to K-pop singer Song Min-ho after he was convicted of violating the country's military service law.

The 33-year-old member of the boy band Winner was found to have been absent multiple times at a community centre in Seoul, where he had worked as a social worker from 2023 to 2024.

All able-bodied men in South Korea have to serve at least 18 months in the military. But some are alternatively assigned as social service personnel for health reasons.

The prison sentence handed on Thursday is suspended for two years. That means he can avoid incarceration if he does not commit any crime during that two-year probationary period.

The court heard that Song, who is also known by his stage name Mino, had recorded 102 unauthorised absences during his 21-month stint as a social service agent.

Military service is a duty to be performed "faithfully", and social service agents are "no exception", the court said.

But the court also noted that Song had admitted to the charges and shown remorse.

Authorities launched an investigation into Song shortly after he was discharged in 2024, when local media reported that he was frequently absent from his social service duties and took excessive sick leave.

Song's supervisor at the social service centre was also given a suspended jail sentence for helping him dodge his duties, including falsifying records to make it look like Song had reported to work.

The conscription of South Korea's entertainers has long been a topic of national public debate.

Gangnam Style singer Psy famously had to enlist twice, once in 2003 and another time in 2007, after a Seoul court ruled that he had neglected his duties by continuing his showbiz activities during his first national service stint.

Steve Yoo, one of the country's biggest pop stars in the 1990s and early 2000s, was embroiled in a national scandal after he was found to have evaded military service in 2002. South Korean authorities banned him from the country after he renounced his citizenship and became a US national shortly before he was due to serve in the military.

Going on hiatus to serve in the military is often a threat for budding careers in South Korea's fast-moving entertainment industry. But the evasion of military service also comes with intense public scrutiny and legal repercussions.

Ahead of the ruling on Thursday, Song told reporters that he regretted his actions and was "sorry toward the people who gave me so much love", Seoul Economic Daily reported.

But he did not answer a question about whether he would re-enlist to serve the mandatory duty.

Entertainment.title: Rochdale Council wins 'Downton Shabby' High Court case
Entertainment.text:
An American man has lost his legal bid to take ownership of a historic mansion for £1.

Hopwood DePree, who claims ancestral links to the Grade II-listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton, Rochdale, said he was "incredibly disappointed" after a judge at the High Court in Manchester ruled against him.

DePree, an actor and filmmaker, argued a 2017 agreement with Rochdale Council gave him the option to buy the manor house after securing planning permission to restore and redevelop it.

However, Judge David Hodge KC found the conditions required for ownership of the property to transfer had not been met.

Despite its current state, Hopwood Hall was described as being in the top 10% of most important listed buildings in England, the court heard.

DePree's plans included a wedding venue, hotel accommodation and visitor attractions aimed at bringing the hall back to life.

However, Rochdale Council decided in 2022 not to transfer ownership of the hall to DePree and later locked him and a group of volunteers out of the site.

The court heard the legal costs were about £150,000, with the council expected to seek an order requiring DePree to pay them.

A Rochdale Council spokesperson said the council was pleased with the judgment.

"It's a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested in this process could have been better spent on the hall itself," they said.

The spokesperson said more than £1.6m had been spent on the hall by the council and Historic England since 2017, and that investment in vital repairs would continue while its long-term future was "considered in due course".

They added that, once restored and refurbished, the building would be "used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton's rich and varied heritage".

DePree published a book about his campaign to restore the hall in 2022, titled Downton Shabby.

Speaking after the ruling, he said he was "incredibly disappointed" and described it as "a sad day".

He said he was discussing next steps with his legal team, adding: "We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved."

"I am getting messages from around the world from people offering money and support," he added.

Entertainment.title: Harry and Meghan: Photographer spotted near Archie and Lilibet's school as Sussexes condemn 'reckless intrusion'
Entertainment.text:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have accused an international photographer of "extraordinary recklessness" for looking into the grounds of the school attended by their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

Two men, both wearing backpacks, were spotted circling the perimeter of the school, with police later identifying one of them as an international press photographer.

A spokesman for Prince Harry and Meghan called it "an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children".

Harry, Meghan, and their children returned to the UK last month after living in California for six years.

The BBC understands that the two men were observed by both private security and school staff on Monday morning, stopping at various points and looking into the school grounds, before returning to a van which police later established was a rental vehicle.

One of the men was later identified as photographer for a European press agency.

"The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless," Harry and Meghan's spokesman said.

"There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day."

The spokesman continued: "Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school."

The children began school in the UK at the start of September, but changed after a few days after security concerns were raised about traffic during the school run.

Earlier this month, it emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their move back.

BreakingNewsTab.title: US says Europe should ready fuel supplies as Trump threatens diesel ban
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he mulls a ban on US exports of the fuel amid a global shortage.

The comments followed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging Europe to immediately ready and release such supplies, arguing that US "farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

The US has threatened to restrict diesel exports amid surging costs due to the war in Iran. The issue is top of mind for US voters ahead of the crucial midterm elections.

On Thursday, the UK held talks with European partners about the potential release of diesel reserves in response to any ban.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.

"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.

On Thursday Trump added that he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves, while Bessent said they should do so "immediately".

"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent said in a post on social media.

The plans come weeks ahead of November elections in the US, where control of Congress will be up for grabs. The president is set to travel across the US campaigning for Republicans in hopes of keeping control of the House and Senate.

Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

UK Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.
