articles.title: Celebrity Traitors: Chaos, coffins and ‘Claudiapatra’ steal the show
articles.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir.

Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities.

"That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged.

"Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen.

Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance", but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour.

"It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said.

But the main talking point of this show was actor Richard E Grant, with his shocking admission.

Grant and presenter Maya Jama were selected as two of Winkleman's three traitors.

But immediately afterwards, Grant appeared to forget the entire point of the game, by gleefully blurting out to those around him he was actually a traitor.

You could have heard a pin drop after he said it. Stunned silence.

"It's an interesting angle," laughed singer James Blunt just afterwards, while comic Rob Beckett told him: "I think you've just done something that's never happened in the game - it is a bold strategy."

Grant later admitted, in footage for viewers of the show: "That may be the biggest mistake I have ever made in my life. I was so thrilled to have been chosen as a traitor that in my unguarded excitement, I said, 'Of course I'm a traitor'.

"I clearly need to defuse all the heat that's coming in my direction."

Ex-BBC journalist Amol Rajan swooped the following day, asking Grant: "What happened last night?"

But instead of sowing clever seeds of doubt, Grant said he'd been so "blatant" about wanting to be a traitor that he simply responded he was one, when he was asked.

It was an odd reply, perhaps because he was flustered.

Rajan labelled him the "Lord of Chaos", but Hall stayed loyal.

"I just don't believe Richard's a traitor, I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour," she said.

"He says and does eccentric things, he's an amazing guy, but I think he's acting out because he's not been chosen."

Hall's loyalty could be tested though, given Alan Carr murdered Paloma Faith in series one by touching her face.

Comic and writer Miranda Hart also thinks Grant could be a faithful, but admitted she is confused.

Winkleman told the press launch she thought Grant blurted out his identity in error, because he was so thrilled to be a traitor.

"He was giddy, wasn't he? He's just laughing at what's happening. Fantastic," she said.

Ed Gamble, the host of BBC One and BBC Sounds spin-off show Uncloaked, added: "It felt like he'd been given the lead role in a film and he just had to tell everyone. It's such an insane moment."

Grant may find that no one tells him a secret ever again.

He did eventually decide to let the much more cool, calm and collected Jama take the lead in their subsequent decision making.

Meanwhile the other celebrities also proved their worth on the show, not least "hard man" Ross Kemp, the former EastEnders actor-turned documentary-maker, whose programmes have focused on gangs and the armed forces.

Having admitted how nervous he was in the pews of the church, he came into his own for the task, along with ex-army captain James Blunt.

They divided the celebrities into teams, leading them to successfully find the treasure on the pirate ship, bagging £15,000.

But Kemp quickly crumbled back in the castle, when paranoia set in.

The Last of Us and Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey, a key player in the task, had grabbed a captain's hat from the boat. They playfully planted it on Kemp's head, marking their victory.

Little Mix's Leigh-Anne Pinnock then touched Kemp on the arm as she walked through the bar.

Clearly remembering how Carr killed off Faith early on, Kemp got understandably fearful he had been killed by a traitor.

This tickled Gamble, who said: "It is one of the funniest things I've ever seen - the moment he gets touched on the arm, having already thought Bella Ramsey putting a captain's hat on him is a murder in plain sight.

"What a variety of men live within the Ross Kemp sphere.

"He's a big hard man running that mission. And then immediately terrified of a member of Little Mix touching him on the arm. That's incredible."

We also learned that although quite a few celebrities wanted to be traitors, including Rajan and Beckett, comics James Acaster and Hart and mathematician Hannah Fry wanted to be faithfuls - Fry said she was "dripping with prefect energy".

Meanwhile YouTuber King Kenny and actress Myha'la had their own strategies.

"I have an innocent face; I want to avenge Niko [Omilana, the first to be banished in series one]. He left too early," Kenny said, while Myha'la added she wants to be perceived as "doughy-eyed, fun, and maybe a little naïve", unlike her scheming character in Industry.

Fashion is likely to be another talking point in the castle.

Beckett observed that when actress Julie Hesmondhalgh wore the shield she'd won, she looked like a "cardinal" in her long, red dress, adding: "I thought we were in the Vatican!"

True to form, Joe Lycett wore a polka-dot shorts suit with a purple feather collar.

Hall was also keen to strut her stuff, saying she wanted to stay long enough to "wear all my fabulous outfits".

Blunt deadpanned: "Well, look, if you go early, I'll wear your outfits."

But although the one-liners were flying, the show got very serious at the end, when the game's new twist dictated that Grant and Jama had to select their third traitor.

They had to choose two celebrities to meet them in person, to argue why they should stay, with the winner joining them and the loser becoming the show's first murder victim.

"They'll beg – there is a God. I'm loving it. Delicious," Grant said, grinning like a kid in a sweet shop.

Rajan and Acaster were chosen, having both put pressure on Grant over being a traitor.

"Amol is the biggest Rottweiler on me; it would take the heat off me for having been such a plonker," he admitted, while adding: "James Acaster is laser-eyed in his conviction that I am a traitor."

Despite wanting to be a faithful, Acaster argued a solid case to stay, telling Grant: "If I go tonight, the first person they're looking at is you."

Rajan then took the floor, saying: "I do think I am uniquely placed to take the heat off you. I'm here because I sniff out liars for a living.

"The faithful think I will identify the traitor by doing my job really well. If I'm on your side, I'll throw them off the scent."

Taking the episode full circle, they each laid in a coffin, just as Winkleman had, to await their fate.

"I'm "90% that nice, warm guy who's on the news, but I'm also 10% psychopath," Rajan had said earlier.

Although his Machiavellian side wasn't apparent when I sat opposite him for years at the BBC, it will be interesting to see what sort of a traitor he is - if he emerges from his coffin.

articles.title: Naomi Campbell wins appeal over charity ban
articles.text:
Model Naomi Campbell has won her appeal against a ban on being a charity trustee, after a tribunal ruled that she was unaware of misconduct at her charity Fashion for Relief.

Campbell was banned from being a charity trustee for five years in 2024 after a watchdog found that Fashion for Relief funds had been spent on luxury hotels and spa treatments.

However, a tribunal said on Thursday, external that the most serious instances of misconduct in the charity "were concealed" from Campbell by a fellow trustee.

"Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct," the three-person tribunal panel said.

The supermodel set up Fashion for Relief to help victims of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and went on to front further campaigns for disasters and causes around the world.

However, the charity was shut in 2023 and Campbell and two other trustees were banned the following year after a Charity Commission inquiry found "serious mismanagement and/or misconduct" at Fashion for Relief, which was not passing on as much of the money raised as it was supposed to.

Campbell appealed, saying one of her fellow trustees, lawyer Bianka Hellmich, forged her signature and impersonated her using a fake email address to misdirect money that was intended for the charity.

Her "only mistake" was trusting Hellmich, Campbell told the tribunal in June.

Hellmich has denied the allegations.

The Charity Commission opposed Campbell's challenge and said the five-year ban should be upheld.

In its ruling, the First-Tier Tribunal panel said Campbell's claim that she was deceived had been corroborated by documentary evidence.

"For the avoidance of doubt, we accept that both Ms Campbell's evidence, as well as her conduct during the operation of the Charity, was entirely honest," they said.

They said Campbell did not know €4,386 (£3,750) of hotel charges from a trip to the south of France in 2018 - including €1,298 (£1,100) for dinner room service, €1,163 (£990) for spa treatments and €112 (£95) for cigarettes - had come out of the charity's expenses.

"The panel is satisfied that Ms Campbell was not responsible for the inappropriate use of the charity's resources or any unjustified expenditure, nor did she contribute or facilitate it," they said.

Campbell must take some responsibility for failures to maintain minutes and file accounts on time - but that was not enough to disqualify the model as a charity trustee, the tribunal said.

"There was serious misconduct and mismanagement in the administration of the charity she founded, Fashion for Relief," the ruling said.

"The Tribunal has found, however, that its most serious features, including unauthorised payments to Ms Campbell's co-trustee, Bianka Hellmich, failures in the management of the Charity's finances and the misuse of its funds, resulted from Ms Hellmich's conduct and were concealed from Ms Campbell."

Unauthorised payments of more than £290,000 were made to Hellmich for apparent consultancy fees, the inquiry found.

The tribunal ruling continued: "Ms Hellmich deceived Ms Campbell, used forged documents and a false email address purporting to belong to her, and also deceived professional advisers and the Commission.

"Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct.

"The Tribunal finds that she had no reasonable basis to suspect Ms Hellmich's dishonesty before regulatory concerns emerged and, when they did, Ms Campbell took reasonable steps in response."

Following the judgment, Campbell thanked the tribunal and the judges "for taking the time to hear my side, look at the evidence, and see the truth of what happened".

The supermodel said: "Giving back has been part of who I am, so having that questioned hurt deeply.

"Now I can get back to what matters most to me: being there for the people and communities I've always wanted to serve.

"Thank you to my higher power."

BBC News has tried to contact Hellmich.

In April 2025, she told the Financial Times, external: "It is deeply distressing that Naomi Campbell is making these false accusations.

"Her claims are a device carefully designed to paint her as a victim, while scapegoating a so-called friend.

"This is testament to the sort of behaviour I endured during this difficult and damaging relationship. I have fully co-operated with the Charity Commission over the past six years.

"I am grateful this challenging period of my life is over. I hope that Naomi finds peace and happiness in her future."

On Thursday, a Charity Commission spokesperson said: "We made the disqualification order for Ms Campbell based on the evidence available to us at the time.

"The court recognised that Ms Campbell, the Commission and the law firm concerned were subject to sophisticated deception by one of the other trustees. This was referred to the Metropolitan Police when we became aware.

"We acknowledge and will reflect on the court's decision and are considering any wider implications for our work."

The Charity Commission also said its intervention ensured other charities including Save the Children received almost £250,000 that was owed to them.

articles.title: Esther Rantzen: The story behind Nicholas Winton on That's Life!
articles.text:
Dame Esther Rantzen, who has died at the age of 86, will perhaps be best remembered for presenting the BBC series That's Life! While the programme ran for two decades, one episode in particular stands out for many.

She presented the hugely popular BBC One show from 1973 to 1994, drawing in huge audiences.

One of Dame Esther's most memorable career moments came during an episode in 1988 - the footage of which has gone viral several times over in recent years.

Dame Esther had been told the story of Nicholas Winton, the man who had organised the rescue of 669 children from Czechoslovakia, which was occupied in 1939 by Nazi forces.

Sir Nicholas was able to rescue the mainly Jewish cohort of children after briefly visiting Prague.

He was knighted in 2003 for his humanitarian work.

Sir Nicholas, who was born to German-Jewish parents, made a list of the children that needed sponsorship and found homes for them to go to in Britain.

He worked alongside activists and humanitarians , externalin Czechoslovakia to navigate complex political obstacles, such as getting children to Britain through the Netherlands, which had closed its borders to Jewish refugees.

Sir Nicholas was ultimately successful due to a House of Commons ruling on allowing young refugees in the country, which had been passed a couple of months before his rescue mission began.

With the help of his mother, he put photos of the children in British magazines such as Picture Post to help find them homes and organised for hostels to take in some refugees too.

He managed to raise money to cover travel for the children and provide them with essentials when they reached British soil.

His incredible work went largely unreported for nearly 50 years - until his wife found a scrapbook in their loft, which contained names of children he had rescued.

It was given to Holocaust researchers, who helped track down some of the children he had helped.

Sir Nicholas' story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988 and Dame Esther Rantzen told viewers about his story.

Speaking in February 2024, Dame Esther said when she first got in touch with Sir Nicholas, who she called Nicky, she "congratulated him on his extraordinary achievement".

She told The Radio Times, external he had expressed some disappointment about his efforts, commenting that "not enough" people had been saved.

"I was devastated that he felt he had failed. I wanted to prove to this extraordinary man that every life he had saved was precious," Dame Esther added.

She invited him onto That's Life and during his first appearance, his scrapbook was shared with the audience, and two women he had saved as children - Vera Gissing and Lady Milena Grenfell-Baines - revealed their identities to him on TV.

They were sitting either side of Sir Nicholas, who had no idea of the surprise - something Dame Esther recalled as "incredibly moving".

Lady Milena is one of the most well-recognised Holocaust survivors in the UK.

She left Prague with her younger sister Eva at the age of nine, travelling on a special train arranged by Winton.

The two sisters were looked after by a Tameside family until their mother arrived the following year, having escaped via Norway.

Gissing, who was rescued from Prague in 1939 at the age of 11, lost most of her family during the Holocaust and ended up settling in the UK after the war ended.

"That was the only time in my career when I had to stop recording to wipe away my tears," Dame Esther also said.

The production team at That's Life were then contacted by several viewers who had watched the show and realised their connection to Sir Nicholas.

That gave the show's team an idea which would go on to become one of British television's most famous moments.

"In our next episode, I asked all those who owed their lives to him to stand, and Nicky, whom we had seated on the front row, turned to see the whole ground floor of the Television Theatre on their feet," Dame Esther recalled.

This is a TV moment many will remember and in subsequent years has been rediscovered by new audiences thanks to social media.

Dame Esther said she watched the episode "many times" and "each time found myself deeply moved".

She says she kept in contact with Sir Nicholas, meeting regularly until his death in 2015 at the age of 106.

They would always have a connection due to the TV show, but Dame Esther said hearing the stories of the children he had saved also made her feel "immensely lucky" to have been a Jew born in England in the 1940s.

Sir Nicholas' work has been the subject of a number of different films and documentaries, most recently the biopic One Life.

Starring Sir Anthony Hopkins, the film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival and was released in the UK in January 2024.

Dame Esther said it had been estimated "that 6, 000 people owe their very existence to Nicholas Winton".

She added: "The Jewish children Nicky rescued were almost the only ones in Czechoslovakia to survive the Holocaust".

And thanks to Dame Esther relaying his story to viewers on That's Life!, millions of people are now aware of the huge impact Sir Nicholas had.

articles.title: First Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in under 30 minutes
articles.text:
The first batch of tickets for Glastonbury Festival have sold out in less than 30 minutes, according to the organisers.

The event will take place from 23-27 June 2027 at Worthy Farm in Pilton, Somerset, after a fallow year in 2026.

Coach tickets have now sold out after less than half an hour, after going on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday. General admission tickets go on sale at 09:00 BST on Sunday morning.

Jessi Dimmock from Glasto Cast, a podcast covering the festival, said: "It's the most stressful weekend of my year. I'll be there Sunday morning with my phone, my laptop, and my coffee and I will be stressed."

Festival organisers announced the first sell out in a post on Instagram.

General admission tickets are £408 for the 2027 festival. Dimmock said that she understands some people might "wince" at the higher prices.

"Anyone who has been to Glastonbury, it is magical. The small things are what makes it. It's just chaos in the best way," she added.

"I just think you can't count how much it is worth it for that money when you think of it in that respect.

"But I do understand, seeing it written down, you do wince at the fact that it now starts with a four rather than a three."

People who want to buy a ticket on Sunday must have already pre-registered on the Glastonbury Festival website.

In recent years, organisers have introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

Registration closed on 25 September, and will not reopen until after the October ticket sales.

Once on the other side of the queue, people can buy up to six tickets per transaction after paying a deposit.

Anyone who missed the registration deadline or is not able to buy a ticket on Sunday will get another chance during the spring resale.

articles.title: Kanye West's Russia shows cancelled after stadium row
articles.text:
Two stadium gigs in Russia by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, have officially been cancelled.

West had been due to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October.

But there was confusion in the lead-up to the shows, as the venue had said it wouldn't host him for what would have been the biggest show by a western artist since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

In a post on messaging app Telegram, gig organisers Say Agency confirmed the concerts had been cancelled with "sincere regret".

"The Ye concerts in St Petersburg will not be able to take place on the scheduled dates," the Moscow-based agency wrote.

"We will issue an official statement regarding the status of the project and our plans in the near future."

Gazprom Arena said in August that it had not signed a rental agreement with the concert promoters and so the gig could not take place on its site.

Say Agency had said it was working to resolve the issue with the stadium before confirming they could not go ahead.

The stadium also acknowledged it had received complaints about West's performance.

He has recently apologised for multiple antisemitic and pro-Nazi comments in the past, saying he had "lost touch with reality" as a result of his bipolar disorder.

articles.title: Tourette's campaigner John Davidson to watch Scottish Baftas via video link after row over racial slur
articles.text:
Tourette's campaigner John Davidson has asked to watch the Scottish Baftas ceremony via a video link at the venue after he shouted a racial slur during the Bafta Film Awards in February.

The movie I Swear, which tells the story of Davidson growing up with Tourette syndrome in Scotland in the 1980s, has been nominated for seven Scottish Baftas.

It scooped three prizes at the Bafta Film Awards in London in February.

But the event was overshadowed by Davidson, whose condition involves involuntary tics, shouting the N-word at presenters Michael B Jordan and Delroy Lindo.

The BBC later apologised for not editing out the slur from its BBC One broadcast, which was shown on a two-hour delay, and remained on BBC iPlayer until the following day.

Bafta Scotland said it had worked with safeguarding and inclusion experts to allow Davidson to take part in its forthcoming ceremony in Glasgow "in the safest way possible for all".

It said Davidson, who was awarded an MBE in 2019 for his work in raising awareness of Tourette's, had suggested watching from a separate room in the venue with his family and friends.

Davidson, from Galashiels, shouted loudly several times before and during the Bafta ceremony in February.

He later said he was "deeply mortified if anyone considers my involuntary tics to be intentional or to carry any meaning".

"I have spent my life trying to support and empower the Tourette's community and to teach empathy, kindness and understanding from others and I will continue to do so," he said in a statement.

"I chose to leave the auditorium early into the ceremony as I was aware of the distress my tics were causing."

At the time, Bafta thanked Davidson for his "dignity and consideration of others, on what should have been a night of celebration for him".

"We take full responsibility for putting our guests in a very difficult situation and we apologise to all," it added.

"We will learn from this and keep inclusion at the core of all we do, maintaining our belief in film and storytelling as a critical conduit for compassion and empathy."

articles.title: Sexual assault charges dismissed against Trailer Park Boys actor
articles.text:
A judge in Nova Scotia, Canada, has dismissed the sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith.

The trial was set to begin in provincial court in Dartmouth on Thursday, but after the Crown provided no evidence against Smith, the actor's attorneys requested the case be dismissed.

The 54-year-old actor, who plays the character Bubbles on the Canadian sitcom, was charged last year for an alleged sexual assault in 2017.

Prosecutor Bryson McDonald told reporters outside court that the Crown offered no evidence in relation to the charge "based on the Crown's ongoing assessment that the prosecution standard has no longer been met".

McDonald would not go into further detail about the standard not being met or why, but said his office has been in regular communication with the complainant throughout the process.

There is a publication ban in place protecting the identity of the complainant.

The complainant said in a statement to Canadian broadcaster CBC that the trial was dismissed because she is "unwilling to sacrifice my mental health" by testifying.

Trailer Park Boys Incorporated, the company behind the show, said in a statement that because the charge against Smith was dropped, the actor will resume his responsibilities with the company.

Smith's attorney also said his client is "pleased that this matter is now behind him and is ready to move forward".

In February, Smith pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault.

Set in a fictional trailer park in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, Trailer Park Boys follows the adventures of three longtime friends and petty criminals.

The Canadian mockumentary series first began airing in 2001 before ending in 2007, but was later revived by Netflix. Season 13 is expected to be released in the coming months.

articles.title: Dame Esther Rantzen: Tributes paid to 'inspirational' presenter and Childline founder
articles.text:
Dame Esther Rantzen was "an inspirational individual" who was "quite a force" as a campaigner, according to the director of Childline, the children's helpline founded by the broadcaster in the 1980s.

"She inspired people, she energised people, she persuaded people," Shaun Friel told BBC Breakfast. "She had a great mind and she had obviously that natural journalistic ability."

Dame Esther, who died on Wednesday at the age of 86, was known for presenting BBC consumer show That's Life! for 21 years, and for campaigning on issues including child welfare and assisted dying.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham led the tributes, saying the veteran broadcaster had "changed countless lives".

BBC director general Matt Brittin also paid tribute to Dame Esther, describing her as a "legend of British broadcasting" whose contribution to public life was "immeasurable".

"Her warmth, spirit and fight for justice and action that we saw on our screens continued long after the programme ended, with a lifetime of campaigning where she changed the lives of millions," he said.

Fellow broadcaster and money saving expert Martin Lewis called Dame Esther an "inspiration" and a "pioneer" whose "impact and memory will long continue to shine".

Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, which runs Childline, said Dame Esther had gone to "exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help".

Dame Esther set up the telephone helpline in 1986 after featuring a number of incidents of child abuse and neglect on That's Life! and realising that many children had nowhere to turn.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Friel said: "The legacy that Dame Esther created when she created Childline is something quite incredible. She changed how society looked upon children."

He added: "When she decided she had a vision or something had to be done or had to be changed, she was quite a force."

TV executive Michael Grade paid tribute to "her courage and her fortitude and what she achieved in her life".

Lord Grade told BBC Radio 4's Today: "She used her television fame to help an awful lot of people, particularly the children. And Childline goes on today, getting so many calls from distressed and abused children.

"That was an extraordinary effort of will to turn the television programme into a long-lasting charity that's so effective and so needed. That's her legacy for me. I'll always remember her for that."

Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006. In 2013, Dame Esther founded The Silver Line to help older people suffering from isolation and loneliness.

She also led campaigns on car safety, organ donation and bullying, and later in life became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.

She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic, but last month said she was now "too physically fragile to make the journey".

Burnham said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life".

Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners.

Baroness Jan Royall, former leader of the House of Lords and a friend of Dame Esther, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that she was a "formidable" person.

"She was an extraordinary, compassionate woman, a passionate woman, and she brought about such change in our world, change for the better."

Baroness Royall added that Dame Esther had "a wicked sense of humour" and a "zest for life", which was the thing that "drove her to try and improve people's lives through Silver Line, Childline etc, but also with the assisted dying bill."

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told Radio 4's Today: "I was lucky enough to know her for more than 50 years, and what I remember is her energy, her intelligence, her resilience. Her vulgar streak, which she enjoyed and she said she got from her mother. She was formidable and she was fun."

Dame Esther told him her campaigning was rooted in memories of difficult times in her own life as a child during and after World War Two, Brandreth said.

Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning.

"She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said.

Dame Elaine Paige, known for her roles in West End productions like Cats and Evita, paid tribute to a "great broadcaster, journalist and campaigner".

She said: "Her Childline, the confidential counselling service for young people in distress, helped so many children and The Silver Line was aimed at older people suffering loneliness and isolation."

Anton Du Beke, Dame Esther's partner on Strictly Come Dancing, shared a photo of the pair dancing together in the 2004 series, writing that the two had "remained firm friends" ever since.

He praised her "breadth of knowledge and passion" and called her "the ultimate breaker of the glass ceiling", adding: "She will be greatly missed and my sincere thoughts are with her family."

Davina McCall wrote on Instagram that Dame Esther had "made the world a better place, and inspired so many of us to do better and live life to its fullest."

The message accompanied a video of the former Big Brother host discussing how Dame Esther was an "inspiration to girls like me when we were growing up".

Presenter Amol Rajan said Dame Esther "changed the course of millions of lives" as he paid tribute, calling her "an inspirational, strong woman ahead of her time".

"Not bad for a bright, Hertfordshire girl born during the early stages of the Second World War."

articles.title: Song Min-ho: K-pop star convicted of violating military service law
articles.text:
A South Korean court has handed a suspended one-year prison sentence to K-pop singer Song Min-ho after he was convicted of violating the country's military service law.

The 33-year-old member of the boy band Winner was found to have been absent multiple times at a community centre in Seoul, where he had worked as a social worker from 2023 to 2024.

All able-bodied men in South Korea have to serve at least 18 months in the military. But some are alternatively assigned as social service personnel for health reasons.

The prison sentence handed on Thursday is suspended for two years. That means he can avoid incarceration if he does not commit any crime during that two-year probationary period.

The court heard that Song, who is also known by his stage name Mino, had recorded 102 unauthorised absences during his 21-month stint as a social service agent.

Military service is a duty to be performed "faithfully", and social service agents are "no exception", the court said.

But the court also noted that Song had admitted to the charges and shown remorse.

Authorities launched an investigation into Song shortly after he was discharged in 2024, when local media reported that he was frequently absent from his social service duties and took excessive sick leave.

Song's supervisor at the social service centre was also given a suspended jail sentence for helping him dodge his duties, including falsifying records to make it look like Song had reported to work.

The conscription of South Korea's entertainers has long been a topic of national public debate.

Gangnam Style singer Psy famously had to enlist twice, once in 2003 and another time in 2007, after a Seoul court ruled that he had neglected his duties by continuing his showbiz activities during his first national service stint.

Steve Yoo, one of the country's biggest pop stars in the 1990s and early 2000s, was embroiled in a national scandal after he was found to have evaded military service in 2002. South Korean authorities banned him from the country after he renounced his citizenship and became a US national shortly before he was due to serve in the military.

Going on hiatus to serve in the military is often a threat for budding careers in South Korea's fast-moving entertainment industry. But the evasion of military service also comes with intense public scrutiny and legal repercussions.

Ahead of the ruling on Thursday, Song told reporters that he regretted his actions and was "sorry toward the people who gave me so much love", Seoul Economic Daily reported.

But he did not answer a question about whether he would re-enlist to serve the mandatory duty.

articles.title: Rochdale Council wins 'Downton Shabby' High Court case
articles.text:
An American man has lost his legal bid to take ownership of a historic mansion for £1.

Hopwood DePree, who claims ancestral links to the Grade II-listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton, Rochdale, said he was "incredibly disappointed" after a judge at the High Court in Manchester ruled against him.

DePree, an actor and filmmaker, argued a 2017 agreement with Rochdale Council gave him the option to buy the manor house after securing planning permission to restore and redevelop it.

However, Judge David Hodge KC found the conditions required for ownership of the property to transfer had not been met.

Despite its current state, Hopwood Hall was described as being in the top 10% of most important listed buildings in England, the court heard.

DePree's plans included a wedding venue, hotel accommodation and visitor attractions aimed at bringing the hall back to life.

However, Rochdale Council decided in 2022 not to transfer ownership of the hall to DePree and later locked him and a group of volunteers out of the site.

The court heard the legal costs were about £150,000, with the council expected to seek an order requiring DePree to pay them.

A Rochdale Council spokesperson said the council was pleased with the judgment.

"It's a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested in this process could have been better spent on the hall itself," they said.

The spokesperson said more than £1.6m had been spent on the hall by the council and Historic England since 2017, and that investment in vital repairs would continue while its long-term future was "considered in due course".

They added that, once restored and refurbished, the building would be "used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton's rich and varied heritage".

DePree published a book about his campaign to restore the hall in 2022, titled Downton Shabby.

Speaking after the ruling, he said he was "incredibly disappointed" and described it as "a sad day".

He said he was discussing next steps with his legal team, adding: "We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved."

"I am getting messages from around the world from people offering money and support," he added.

articles.title: Harry and Meghan: Photographer spotted near Archie and Lilibet's school as Sussexes condemn 'reckless intrusion'
articles.text:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have accused an international photographer of "extraordinary recklessness" for looking into the grounds of the school attended by their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

Two men, both wearing backpacks, were spotted circling the perimeter of the school, with police later identifying one of them as an international press photographer.

A spokesman for Prince Harry and Meghan called it "an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children".

Harry, Meghan, and their children returned to the UK last month after living in California for six years.

The BBC understands that the two men were observed by both private security and school staff on Monday morning, stopping at various points and looking into the school grounds, before returning to a van which police later established was a rental vehicle.

One of the men was later identified as photographer for a European press agency.

"The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless," Harry and Meghan's spokesman said.

"There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day."

The spokesman continued: "Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school."

The children began school in the UK at the start of September, but changed after a few days after security concerns were raised about traffic during the school run.

Earlier this month, it emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their move back.
